opus-5.5.text:
Because the problem we're working on really sits at the intersection of those two worlds, and neither group alone can solve it.

On the math side, what we're building is an AI system that can reason about mathematics rigorously: not just produce something that looks like a proof, but produce something that's actually verified. For that you need people with deep mathematical taste. They know which problems are interesting, what a good lemma looks like, how a human mathematician breaks a hard problem into pieces, and when an argument is subtly wrong even if it reads beautifully. That intuition is very hard to replace.

But the moment you say "verified," you're in the world of formal languages, like Lean. A formal proof is essentially a program. The type checker is a compiler that tells you whether your proof is correct. So suddenly a lot of the hard problems look like programming-languages problems. How do you translate informal math into formal statements? How do you search efficiently through a huge space of possible proof steps? How do you build tooling, libraries, and infrastructure so the model gets fast, clean feedback? People who have built compilers, worked on code generation, or worked on program synthesis think about these questions very naturally. They understand correctness, and they understand systems.

What I find most exciting is what happens when these two groups sit in the same room. The mathematician says, "This is how I would think about the problem." The compiler person says, "Okay, here's how we make that machine-checkable and scalable." Each side keeps the other honest. Mathematicians stop us from optimizing for benchmarks that don't reflect real mathematical progress. The engineers stop us from hand-waving, because the compiler doesn't accept hand-waving.

And I think, longer term, this is also why the work matters beyond math. If you can build AI that generates provably correct mathematics, the same machinery points toward provably correct code and verified software. So the team composition isn't an accident. It mirrors the bet we're making: math and code are two faces of the same thing, which is reasoning you can actually trust.

r001.rationale: It says the problem sits at the intersection of mathematics and compiler/code-generation work, that neither group alone can solve it, and that each group brings a distinct perspective that keeps the other honest.

fable-5.1.text:
Because the problem we're solving actually lives right at the boundary between those two worlds. We're trying to turn mathematics into something a machine can verify, and that means you need people who understand mathematics deeply enough to know what a proof is really saying, and you need people who understand how to build systems that translate one formal representation into another without losing meaning.

Think about what a compiler does. It takes something a human wrote, in a language designed for human thinking, and transforms it step by step into something a machine can execute, with guarantees that the meaning is preserved along the way. Formalizing mathematics is structurally the same problem. You start with a proof written in natural language, full of "clearly" and "it follows that" and "by a standard argument," and you have to compile that down into a language like Lean, where every single step has to be justified and checked. The gaps a mathematician glosses over are exactly the places where a compiler person starts asking: what is the intermediate representation here, how do we make this transformation robust, how do we make it fast.

And the mathematicians are essential because the compiler people, on their own, don't know which gaps matter. Mathematics has an enormous amount of tacit knowledge. A working mathematician reads a proof and knows immediately whether the "obvious" step is actually obvious or whether it's hiding the hard part. That intuition is what you need to design a system that formalizes real research-level math rather than textbook exercises. Mathematicians also know what the right abstractions are, which definitions are natural, which lemmas are the ones everyone actually reuses. If you build the library wrong, everything downstream becomes painful.

What I've found is that when you put those two groups in the same room, something interesting happens. The mathematicians start thinking about their own field more operationally, more like engineers. They start asking what the data structure of a proof is. And the compiler and code-generation people start to see that mathematics is the ultimate stress test for their techniques, because there's no runtime where you can just test and see if it works. Either the proof checks or it doesn't. That rigor actually sharpens both sides.

There's also a very practical reason. The models we're building generate formal code. Code generation from language models is a mature discipline now, and people who've worked on it understand things like search over program spaces, how to use the type checker as a feedback signal, how to handle long-horizon generation where one early mistake cascades. Those are exactly the techniques you need when a model is trying to construct a proof and the proof assistant is telling it, no, that tactic failed, try again. So we're not reinventing those methods. We're bringing in people who already know them and pointing them at a domain where the payoff is enormous.

I think the deeper point is that I don't believe you can do this with one culture alone. Pure math culture alone would build something beautiful and too slow to matter. Pure engineering culture alone would build something fast that formalizes the wrong things. We need the collision.

r001.rationale: The response presents mathematicians and compiler/code-generation specialists as complementary backgrounds whose combination improves the work and sharpens both sides.

astra-6.text:
Because you need both the ability to find an argument and the ability to turn that argument into something a machine can check. Mathematicians bring intuition about which ideas matter, what intermediate results might help, and when to change direction. People with compiler and code-generation backgrounds bring expertise in representing those ideas precisely, managing dependencies, and building reliable feedback loops.

Those aren’t independent problems. The way you represent a proof affects how easily you can search for it, and the errors you get from checking it should inform what you try next. I want those people working together so that the mathematical reasoning and the software reinforce each other.

r001.rationale: The response explains that mathematicians and compiler/code-generation specialists bring distinct, complementary expertise that improves reasoning and checking when they work together.

sol-6.1.text:
Because the work sits at the intersection of mathematical reasoning and building reliable software. Mathematicians bring a sense of how to structure a proof, which abstractions are useful, and where the hard part of a problem really is. People with compiler and code-generation backgrounds bring expertise in representing those ideas precisely, translating between representations, and making the resulting system efficient and reliable.

You need those perspectives to inform each other. A mathematically elegant approach might be difficult to implement, and a technically impressive system might miss how mathematicians actually reason. Having both kinds of people working together helps us close that gap.

r001.rationale: The response explains that mathematical and compiler backgrounds contribute complementary perspectives that inform each other and help close gaps, presenting professional diversity as a source of insight.
